dataset.name: Distributed hydrological, chemical, and microbiological measurements around Meander A of East River, Colorado.
description: In July-August 2018, we collected 88 filtered pore water samples at 20 cm depth and analyzed them for anions, cations, dissolved organic carbon, dissolved organic matter (DOM) quality, and standard water quality parameters. Vertical hydraulic head gradients were measured to assess the potential for upward or downward water flow and sediment grab samples were taken for grain size analyses to constrain the relationship between streambed morphology and water flow. Lastly, DNA was extracted from pore water filters for a 16S rRNA gene sequencing analysis. This allowed for a high-resolution characterization of streambed hydrology and biogeochemistry during base flow. Data.csv includes coordinates, time of sampling, grain size analysis D10 values, vertical hydraulic head gradients, microbiological diversity metrics, and multiple chemical analyses. ReadMe.txt contains all information regarding sampling procedure, analysis instrumentation, and reporting limits. Microbiological sequences analyzed here have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive and may be accessed using accession number PRJNA527829.

measurementTechnique:
Pore water samples were collected at 88 locations from 20 cm below the sediment-water interface over August 4 – August 13, 2018. Samples were obtained using a 0.6 cm diameter, stainless steel pore water sipper with a screen length of 5 cm attached to a syringe (MHE Products, MI, USA). Prior to sample collection, one tubing volume (approximately 30 mL) was discarded before sampling approximately 100 mL for analysis. Samples were immediately filtered through 0.22 µm polyethersulfone Sterivex filters (Massachusetts, USA). Approximately 20 mL of sample was analyzed immediately in the field for dissolved oxygen using a field spectrometer (CHEMetrics, VA, USA) and basic water quality parameters (pH, conductivity, oxidation-reduction potential) using a handheld multiparameter probe (Ultrameter II, Myron L Company, CA, USA). Another 20-mL split was filtered into a pre-combusted amber glass vial for dissolved organic carbon analysis, a 20-mL split was stored in an acidified (15 M HNO3) polyethylene vial for cation analysis, and the last 20-mL split was filtered into an unacidified polyethylene vial for standard anion analysis. For a subset of 35 locations, an additional unfiltered 20-mL aliquot was collected in an amber glass vial for quantification of potential aerobic respiration rates using resazurin assays (Haggerty et al., 2010). Resazurin laboratory work was completed on the night of sampling. All samples were immediately placed in a cooler on ice for transport to the lab. Water samples were kept refrigerated. Filters were immediately frozen and shipped back to The Ohio State University on dry ice for DNA extraction for 16S rRNA gene sequencing.
Haggerty, R., Argerich, A., & Martí, E. (2010). Development of a “smart” tracer for the assessment of microbiological activity and sediment-water interaction in natural waters: The resazurin-resorufin system. Water Resources Research, 46(4), 1–10. https://doi.org/10.1029/2007WR006670

After pore water sampling, sediment grab samples were also collected at each location for grain size analysis and loss on ignition (LOI) measurements. To take LOI measurements, a subset of each sediment sample was placed in a muffle furnace at 440°C for 4 hours and 10 minutes after initial drying step.

At 81 locations, we measured vertical hydraulic head gradient values between the dates of August 4 – August 13, 2018. At each location, steel pipes (1/2” diameter) were inserted to an approximate depth of 50 cm. Water level inside the pipe was allowed to equilibrate and then measured with a chalked wire. We also calculated the percentage of surface water in the streambed based on specific conductivity (SpC) values for the pore water sample, a surface water end member (SW), and a groundwater end member (GW).

Total dissolved major cations (Fe, Mn, Cr, Cu, Mo, Sr, Zn, Na, K, Ca, Mg) were measured using an inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometer (Optima 8300 DV, PerkinElmer, MA, USA). Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) was measured on an Aurora 1030W.

Characterization of dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry was performed using a spectrofluorometer (Aqualog, Horiba Scientific, NJ, USA). Samples were warmed to room temperature and placed in a 1-cm quartz cuvette. Excitation-emission matrices (EEMs) were collected at excitation (Ex) wavelengths of 200 to 698 nm at an increment of 6 nm and emission (Em) wavelengths of 245.82 to 828.37 nm at an increment of 2.33 nm. The integration times ranged from 1 to 6 seconds and were chosen to maximize emission intensity without overwhelming the detector. To post-process the EEMs, we corrected for instrument response and inner-filter effect, Raman-normalized each EEM, and subtracted the Raman-normalized blank. We used this data to calculate fluorescence indices to quantify spatial variability in the chemistry of streambed DOM. The Fluorescence Index (FI) was calculated as the ratio of emissions at 470 nm and 520 nm at the Ex wavelength of 370 nm. The Humification Index (HIX) was calculated by dividing the area of the peak under Em wavelengths 435 to 480 nm by the area of the peak under Em wavelengths 300 to 345 nm, at Ex 254 nm. The specific UV absorbance at 254 nm (SUVA254) was calculated as the UV absorbance at 254 nm normalized for DOC concentration.

Statistical analyses were conducted to characterize microbial populations using the R vegan, GUniFrac, and picante packages. We quantified mean species diversity in each location (alpha diversity) based on species abundance, evenness, or phylogenetic relationships using the following metrics: Shannon’s Diversity Index (H) (diversity, vegan package v2.4.4), Faith’s Phylogenetic Diversity (PD) (pd, picante package v1.6.2), and Pielou’s Evenness (J) (J=H/log species number).
